summary: For ages 7–8, children learn that [curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-3] taken apart and rebuilt into a different object, with the same pieces persisting — none created or lost, only rearranged (NGSS 2-PS1-3; DCI PS1.A). The core learning move is hands-on: build, disassemble, rebuild a DIFFERENT object from the SAME pieces, and gather evidence (count and lay out pieces before and after) that the set is unchanged. This is a concrete rehearsal for conservation of matter, kept at the level of visible, countable pieces — not invisible particles. Learner construction is emphasised because the standard asks for first-hand observation; recognition/matching and quiz tasks can check the conclusion but do not by themselves let the child perform the take-apart/rebuild or gather the count evidence.
misconceptions: Believing pieces are 'used up', disappear, or are created when an object is taken apart and rebuilt.
Thinking a rebuilt object is made of brand-new material rather than the same pieces rearranged.
Assuming more/bigger arrangements contain more 'stuff' than the pieces they were built from.
Conflating rearrangement with a change to the pieces themselves (the pieces are transformed), rather than only their configuration changing.
Over-extending to substances that are NOT a small set of discrete pieces (e.g. thinking you can un-mix or un-burn things the same way) — this idea is about reversible reassembly of discrete parts.

activities.title: Build, take apart, rebuild — same pieces, new object
steps: Take a small, countable set of pieces (e.g. 8 building bricks or magnetic tiles) and build one object, such as a robot.
Count every piece in the object, touching each one (or count them before you build), and record the number (e.g. 8). Draw or photograph the pieces so you have a record to check against later.
Take the object fully apart so the pieces are loose and scattered.
Rebuild the SAME pieces into a clearly different object, such as a car.
Count and lay out the pieces again, and compare with your first count: if no piece was dropped, lost or added, the number is the same (8).
Line up the pieces one-to-one against your first count and your drawing or photo of the original pieces to confirm it is the same set — none appeared, none vanished.
Say aloud what changed (the arrangement / the object) and what did not change (the pieces themselves and their count).
activities.insight: The object can disappear and reappear as something completely new, but not one piece is created or lost — the same small set of pieces is simply rearranged. This is evidence-based: you can count and match the pieces to prove it.

activities.title: One box, two creations challenge
steps: Starting from one fixed set of pieces, build two different things, one after the other (e.g. a dog, then a car), using every piece each time.
After each build, confirm the piece count is unchanged.
Describe in words or a drawing that both objects came from exactly the same pieces.
activities.insight: A single small set of pieces can make many different objects — the variety lives in the arrangement, while the set of pieces stays the same.

activities.title: Record and connect to real reuse
steps: Photograph or draw the same pieces in both arrangements, with the matching piece count noted for each.
Make a simple 'same pieces, new object' record sheet showing the before and after builds and the equal counts.

Name an everyday example of reusing pieces to make something new — e.g. dismantling a Lego model to build a new one, or taking apart an old toy and using its wheels and screws to build something different.
Explain why that example is the same idea: the pieces are reused, not made from scratch.
activities.insight: Keeping pieces as pieces and reusing them is something people do in real life; the object changes but the material carries over.

activities.title: Diagnose and discuss: where did the object go?
steps: Observe an adult build an object from 10 pieces, take it apart, and build a different object from the very same pieces.
Before the rebuild is re-counted, PREDICT how many pieces the new object has and WHY.
Answer: 'Did any pieces get made or disappear — how do you know?'
Answer: 'Could you build the exact same first object again from these pieces? What does that tell us?'
Answer the deeper question: 'The first object is gone — so where did it go?'
Try the variant: imagine (or watch) two pieces slipped into a pocket before the rebuild — now what is different, and why?
activities.insight: The count must stay the same because it is the same pieces in a new arrangement. The first object (an arrangement) no longer exists, but every piece (the material) still does — so the original could even be rebuilt. The object ending is not the same as the material vanishing.

checkQuestion: Build a little dog from 10 building bricks in front of the child, then take it apart and build a car from the very same bricks. Ask: 'How many bricks are in the car now? Did any bricks get made or disappear — how do you know?' Then: 'The dog is gone — so where did it go?'
checkAnswer: Ten bricks (the count is unchanged); no bricks were made or lost — the same pieces were rearranged. The 'dog' as an arrangement no longer exists, but every brick still does.
